title: What is known about 1RB1RE_1LC1LA_1RA0LD_1LC0LE_0LF0RA_---1RC
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RE_1LC1LA_1RA0LD_1LC0LE_0LF0RA_---1RC.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, and it is now a question about a small system of events, proved in Lean. This machine is the table of 1RB0RD_1LC0RA_1LF1LD_0RE0LC_---1LB_1RB1RC (bbchallenge 74982) read in a mirror and started in another state. It is a counter ticked once per sweep by a carry automaton. When a carry runs through all the digits it reaches the left end of the tape, and there, for every counter, it either adds a digit, turns all the units at the right end into digits, or halts. The machine halts from blank tape exactly when this event system halts from a one-digit counter (kernel only). The eight overflows so far were extensions and conversions; the last, at step 506,587,790,058, turned 410,923 units into digits. The next one is of the order of 21.3·105 sweeps away, and its kind is not known. The two machines are separate halting questions.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: A halt can only happen at the left end
claims.text: A closed tape language from windows of 4 cells covers the run from blank tape; in it the halting transition F0 can only fire with blank tape to the left of the head. So the machine halts iff F reads a 0 with only blank tape to its left (it can only get there as E0 → 0LF).

claims.title: The same table as 74982, in a mirror
claims.text: Reading the table right to left and renaming the states (A, B, C, D, E, F here are C, F, B, A, D, E of 1RB0RD_1LC0RA_1LF1LD_0RE0LC_---1LB_1RB1RC) gives that machine's table. A step of one is a step of the other on the mirrored tape, so this machine halts from blank tape exactly when 74982 halts from blank tape started in state C. The table of this machine is restated in that Lean file.

claims.title: Every overflow, for every counter
claims.text: The counter is digits on every second cell with a 1 between neighbours and a last cell at the left end. When the carry runs through all the digits and reads the last cell d: in state a, d = 0 becomes 1 and d = 1 gives the counter one more digit; in state b on 0 or state c on 1 the machine halts; in state b on 1 or state c on 0 all the units become counter digits. After each of these the last cell is 1, so from then on the machine halts exactly when a carry reaches the left end in state c.

claims.title: The machine is the event system
claims.text: 16 steps from blank tape the machine is at an arrival with one unit, the single digit 1 and last cell 1. It halts from blank tape if and only if the event system evstep halts from there.

claims.title: The eighth overflow is a conversion of 410,923 units
claims.text: The first 410,975 sweeps of the event system do not halt, and the next one turns a wall of 410,923 units into digits. The machine halts from blank tape if and only if the event system halts from the counter this leaves: 410,922 ones, a 0, the 60 marks of the last carry and a 1 (410,984 digits). The sweeps are evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: The overflows of the run are events of the system
claims.text: The event system gives the machine's own arrivals on the first 200,000 steps, and its events are the overflows found by the run-length simulator: conversions at steps 28, 91, 450, 7,545 and 506,587,790,058 (sweeps 1, 3, 10, 53 and 410,976), extensions at steps 309 and 1,252 (sweeps 8 and 21).

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 36,625 cells have been visited and 18,342 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: 10<sup>16</sup> steps, eight overflows, no halt
claims.text: An exact run-length simulator (c/tok.c; it agrees with tools/c/tmrun.c at step 10,000,208,949) runs 1016 steps (5.8·107 visits of the right end). The head reaches the left end only at steps 3, 28, 91, 309, 450, 1,252, 7,545 and 506,587,790,058, each time in state D, which bounces.

claims.title: Growth shape: fixed/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.495).

claims.title: A binary counter of odd runs
claims.text: Between visits of the right end the head rewrites the odd runs next to the unit block: (1,3)→(5) every other visit, (3,3)→(7) every 4th, (3,1,5)→(7,3) every 8th, and so on, halving: a binary counter of the visits. Its width stays fixed between overflows (123 cells from step 10<sup>4</sup> to 5·10<sup>11</sup>). These rewrites are the carry automaton of 74982 seen on run lengths; the automaton itself is proved for every digit string.

claims.title: The next overflow is out of reach
claims.text: The next overflow needs a carry through 410,984 digits. On small counters the number of sweeps to the next overflow doubles about every 3 digits, which puts it at the order of 2<sup>1.3·10<sup>5</sup></sup> sweeps. The sequence of carry states leaving a prefix of the counter, kept as a straight-line program, stops compressing after about 150 digits (5,000 nodes at 100 digits, 7.3·10<sup>6</sup> at 200), so its kind was not computed.

claims.title: The epoch after step 7,545
claims.text: Between the overflows at steps 7,545 and 5·1011 the tape is a fixed prefix, a reservoir (1,3)^k of run pairs made by the overflow, an active counter region that eats into the reservoir (k = 14, 10, 5, 4, 4, 2, 1, 1, 0 at visits 56, 26..213) and then grows one long run (length 21..33 at visits 212..216), and the units. The numeral system of the active region is not decoded.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. It halts if and only if, at some overflow, the carry reaches the left end in state c. The next overflow is the first chance.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same table as 1RB0RD_1LC0RA_1LF1LD_0RE0LC_---1LB_1RB1RC up to renaming and mirroring, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. This machine is an odometer: every trip of its head adds one to a counter written with runs of ones, and only when the counter rolls over does the head reach the one place where it could stop. Lean proves what every roll-over does: it adds a digit, or turns the long block of units into new digits, or halts. It has rolled over eight times without stopping; the next roll-over is unimaginably far away.

facts.text: From blank tape, for the event system started on a one-digit counter (proved).
The last at step 506,587,790,058 turned 410,923 units into counter digits.
No halt in an exact run-length simulation.

sections.heading: An odometer made of runs
html: Write the tape as the lengths of its runs of 1s (separated by single 0s); u is a run of length 1. The tape is a short prefix, a counter region of short odd runs, and a long block of units that grows by one every time the head reaches the right end:

<svg viewBox="0 0 560 44" role="img" aria-label="prefix, counter, unit block" style="width:100%;max-width:560px;height:auto;font:11px var(--mono);"><text x="120" y="23" text-anchor="end" fill="var(--muted)">tape</text><rect x="126.0" y="8" width="59.4" height="22" rx="3" fill="var(--sunk)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><text x="155.7" y="23" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fg)">prefix</text><rect x="187.4" y="8" width="120.9" height="22" rx="3" fill="var(--accent-soft)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><text x="247.9" y="23" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fg)">counter: odd runs</text><rect x="310.3" y="8" width="243.7" height="22" rx="3" fill="var(--heur-bg)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><text x="432.1" y="23" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fg)">u u u u u u u u ...</text></svg>

On each trip the head walks left over the units, changes the counter a little at its right edge, and walks back. The changes are carries: (1, 3) → (5) happens every other trip, (3, 3) → (7) every 4th, (3, 1, 5) → (7, 3) every 8th, and so on, each kind half as often as the one before. That is exactly how the digits of a binary counter change when you add 1, so the region counts the trips.

sections.heading: Only when the counter rolls over
html: The machine stops only when state F reads a 0, and Lean proves (with a closed tape language from windows of 4 cells) that this can only happen at the very left end of the tape, after state E steps off it. The head gets there only when a carry runs through the whole counter: an overflow, like an odometer going from 999,999 to 1,000,000.

The counter is decoded now. This machine is the table of 74982 read in a mirror, and for that table Lean proves the carry rule for every digit string: three carry states a, b, c walk from the units into the counter, rewriting one digit each. When a carry runs through every digit it reads the last cell at the left end, and one of three things happens:

carry state at the left endwhat happens
athe counter gains a digit
ball the units at the right end become counter digits
cthe machine halts

That has happened eight times. The seven overflows after the first arrival, 16 steps in, were b, b, a, b, a, b, b (at steps 28, 91, 309, 450, 1,252, 7,545 and 506,587,790,058). The last one turned 410,923 units into digits, which is why the tape changed from a long block of units into a wide region of short runs. So the machine halts from blank tape exactly when this little event system, started on a one-digit counter, ever meets state c at the left end (proved in Lean).

Filling the new counter of 410,984 digits takes on the order of 2130,000 trips, so the next chance to stop is far beyond any computer, and no shortcut for finding the carry's state then was found. On random small counters each of the three outcomes is common (observed), which says nothing about this one.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.495).
After 109 steps the tape spans 36,625 cells (10 left of the start, 26,854 right), with a density of 1s of 0.501.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in the other, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

summary: The table of 74982 in a mirror: a counter ticked by a carry automaton, where every overflow adds a digit, turns the units into digits, or halts (proved in Lean for every counter). The machine halts exactly when the event system does from a one-digit counter; the eight overflows so far did not halt, the last (step 5.07·10<sup>11</sup>) made a counter of 410,984 digits, and the next is ~2<sup>1.3·10<sup>5</sup></sup> sweeps away.
family: counter that overflows at the left end
